title: WHAT IF YOUR SPOUSE DOESN’T WANT SEX?
paragraphs:
WHAT IF YOUR SPOUSE DOESN’T WANT SEX?
When Rejection Enters the Bedroom, Desire Becomes Pain, and Marriage Starts Asking Questions Neither of You Knows How to Answer
There is a particular kind of loneliness nobody warns you about before marriage.
It is not sleeping alone.
It is lying six inches away from the person you love and feeling like there are six thousand miles between you.
You reach over.
Nothing.
You try again another night.
“Not tonight.”
Then another.
“I’m tired.”
Another week passes.
Then another month.
Eventually, something changes inside you.
You stop asking because asking hurts.
Or perhaps you are the spouse on the other side.
You see the disappointment in their eyes before they even say anything.
You know what they want.
You know what marriage is “supposed” to look like.
But something inside you has gone quiet.
Maybe you are exhausted.
Maybe resentment has been accumulating underneath conversations that never actually resolve anything.
Maybe childbirth changed your body.
Maybe menopause changed it again.
Maybe stress has hollowed you out.
Maybe medication, hormones, illness, pain, depression, grief, trauma, fear, insecurity, or years of emotional disconnection have affected desires you once assumed would always be there.
Maybe sex stopped feeling like affection and started feeling like an obligation.
Maybe your spouse thinks you are rejecting their body when, deep down, your heart has been screaming about something neither of you has known how to name.
And now both of you are hurting.
One feels unwanted.
The other feels pressured.
One asks, “Why don’t you desire me?”
The other silently wonders, “Do you love me even when I cannot give you what you want?”

This is where marriages can become dangerous places for the soul—not necessarily because somebody committed adultery, filed for divorce, or walked away, but because two wounded people can begin interpreting each other through pain instead of love.
And pain is a terrible translator.
It turns “I’m exhausted” into “You’re unattractive.”
It turns “I miss being close to you” into “You only care about sex.”
It turns silence into accusation.
It turns disappointment into shame.
It turns a bedroom into a courtroom.
But Jesus did not come merely to win arguments between husbands and wives.
He came to redeem sinners.
And sometimes redemption begins when we stop asking, “Who owes whom?” and start asking a far more frightening question:
“How can I love my spouse like Christ when I am hurting?”
That question changes everything.
Scripture does speak directly about sexual intimacy in marriage, and one of the clearest passages is also one of the most frequently mishandled.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:3–4, KJV
The Greek is striking.
Paul uses the expression:
τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω
tēn opheilēn apodidotō
It carries the idea of rendering what is due within the marriage relationship.
But watch what Paul does next, because this matters enormously.
He does not tell the wife that her body simply belongs to her husband and stop there.
He immediately reverses the statement.
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή
Likewise, the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but his wife does.
The structure is radically mutual.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
Not domination.
Not humiliation.
Not, “God says you owe me, so give me what I want.”
Christian marriage is not one person weaponizing Scripture to obtain access to another person's body.
That completely misses the character of the passage.
Paul continues:
“Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time…”
—1 Corinthians 7:5, KJV
The Greek includes:
εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου
ei mēti an ek symphōnou
“Except perhaps by agreement.”
The word συμφώνου — symphōnou carries the idea of mutual agreement or accord. It is related to the idea behind our word “symphony”—voices sounding together.
That matters.
Biblical marital sexuality is not supposed to sound like one voice overpowering another.
There should be mutuality.
Care.
Giving.
Agreement.
Love.
That does not mean persistent sexual rejection is insignificant.
It can hurt terribly.
For some husbands and wives, repeated rejection cuts far deeper than physical frustration.
It whispers:
“You are undesirable.”
“You don't matter.”
“I don't want you anymore.”
And when the person whose acceptance matters most appears to withdraw, insecurity can become brutal.
If that is where you are, your pain should not be mocked.
Wanting sexual intimacy with your spouse is not inherently dirty.
Sexual desire within marriage is not something Christianity needs to apologize for.
God created marriage before sin entered the world.
Genesis says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
—Genesis 2:24, KJV
The Hebrew expression for “one flesh” is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad
“One flesh.”
Jesus Himself later quotes this creation text and says:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh.”
—Matthew 19:6, KJV
Sexual union belongs within that larger covenant reality.
It is physical, but it was never meant to be merely physical.
This is why rejection can feel so personal.
But here is where wounded hearts can make a catastrophic mistake.
Your spouse's body is not medicine for your insecurity.
Sex cannot bear the weight of proving your worth.
Your ultimate identity cannot rest on whether another human being desires you tonight.
Your deepest worth was settled somewhere else.
At a cross.
Where the Son of God loved sinners who could offer Him nothing worthy of His sacrifice.
If your spouse does not want sex, the first question should not automatically be:
“How do I convince them?”
Sometimes the holier question is:
“What happened?”
Those are very different questions.
One seeks access.
The other seeks understanding.
“What happened to us?”
“What are you carrying?”
“Are you hurting?”
“Do you feel safe with me emotionally?”
“Have I neglected you outside the bedroom and then expected closeness inside it?”
“Is sex painful?”
“Are you exhausted?”
“Is there something medical happening?”
“Did something I said wound you?”
“Is there unresolved resentment between us?”
“Do you feel loved when sex is not involved?”
“Is there something you have been afraid to tell me?”
Those questions require courage because the answer might involve you.
Perhaps the problem is not entirely your spouse's libido.
Perhaps there are apologies that have never been spoken.
Perhaps tenderness disappeared long before sex did.
Perhaps your spouse has been starving for conversation while you have been starving for touch.
Perhaps pornography entered the marriage and changed expectations.
Perhaps comparison poisoned attraction.
Perhaps criticism slowly destroyed emotional safety.
Perhaps years of small dismissals became a mountain.
Perhaps neither of you is the villain.
Perhaps you are simply two exhausted human beings who stopped knowing how to reach each other.
This is why Ephesians 5 cannot be reduced to arguments about marital roles.
Paul tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
The Greek word translated “love” is a form of:
ἀγαπάω — agapaō
And Paul does not leave that love undefined.
He points toward Christ.
Christ loved.
Christ gave Himself.
Christian marital love therefore asks something more demanding than, “Am I getting my needs met?”
It asks:
“Am I becoming the kind of spouse who knows how to give?”
And that question belongs to both husband and wife.
Because immediately before Paul's household instructions stands a sentence people sometimes forget:
“Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.”
—Ephesians 5:21, KJV
Marriage is not supposed to become a competition between whose unmet need deserves more sympathy.
Your spouse may need to take your sexual loneliness seriously.
You may need to take your spouse's exhaustion, fear, physical pain, emotional wounds, or diminished desire seriously.
Both can be true.
That is maturity.
You can say:
“This rejection is hurting me deeply.”
without saying:
“Therefore you must give me sex.”
You can say:
“I don't want sex right now.”
without saying:
“Your loneliness doesn't matter to me.”
There is a road between coercion and indifference.
It is called love.
And love tells the truth.
If you are constantly refusing your spouse while refusing to discuss why, something needs attention.
Not condemnation.
Attention.
If your spouse is repeatedly pressuring, shaming, threatening, manipulating, spiritually intimidating, or using Scripture to demand sexual access, something needs attention too.
Marriage does not transform selfishness into holiness merely because somebody can attach a Bible verse to it.
Jesus never taught us to use truth as a weapon for satisfying ourselves.
Look at Christ.
Really look at Him.
He possesses all authority, yet He washes feet.
He is Lord, yet He serves.
He is betrayed, yet He does not become corrupt.
He is rejected, yet rejection does not redefine His identity.
He speaks truth, but truth from His mouth is never permission for selfishness.
This is the Savior standing in the middle of your hurting marriage.
And perhaps the greatest danger in a sexless or sexually struggling marriage is not simply lack of sex.
It is what disappointment can tempt you to become.
Bitter.
Punishing.
Sarcastic.
Cold.
Secretive.
Pornography becomes tempting.
Flirting becomes easier to justify.
An emotional affair begins feeling harmless.
You start imagining another person who would “appreciate you.”
You tell yourself:
“I have needs.”
And suddenly pain starts writing permissions God never wrote.
Be careful.
Your suffering does not make sin safe.
Temptation may explain the battle.
It does not sanctify surrender.
Jesus said:
“Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
—Matthew 26:41, KJV
If rejection has made pornography attractive, bring it into the light.
If you have begun emotionally attaching yourself to somebody who is not your spouse, stop romanticizing it.
If you are secretly messaging someone because they make you feel desired, do not wait until “nothing happened.”
Something is already happening in your heart.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get accountable.
Bring darkness into light before darkness convinces you it is home.
And if you are the spouse who has withdrawn, do not assume the other person's longing is shallow simply because you experience sexuality differently.
Listen.
Your spouse may not merely be saying:
“I want sex.”
They may be saying:
“I miss you.”
“I miss feeling chosen.”
“I miss being close.”
“I am scared that you don't want me anymore.”
Hear the heart underneath the request.
And if you are the spouse longing for intimacy, hear the heart underneath the refusal too.
Perhaps “not tonight” actually means:
“I am overwhelmed.”
“I don't feel beautiful.”
“My body hurts.”
“I am carrying resentment.”
“I need affection that isn't a transaction.”
“I am afraid every touch has to lead somewhere.”
“I need you to see me before you try to have me.”
Imagine what could happen if husbands and wives stopped defending themselves long enough to hear those sentences.
Maybe tonight does not need to end with sex.
Maybe tonight needs to begin with tears.
Maybe you need to sit on the edge of the bed and finally say:
“I don't want to fight anymore. I want to understand you.”
Maybe somebody needs to apologize without adding “but.”
Maybe somebody needs to forgive.

Maybe somebody needs to make a medical appointment because persistent loss of desire, pain during sex, hormonal changes, medication effects, sleep problems, or other health concerns deserve compassionate professional attention rather than shame.
Maybe you need a qualified marriage counselor or therapist who respects your Christian convictions.
Maybe your pastor can help.
Maybe the problem has become too painful to solve with another late-night argument.
Getting appropriate help is not admitting your marriage has failed.
Sometimes asking for help is how you stop pretending everything is fine long enough to begin repairing what isn't.

And if there has been sexual coercion, abuse, threats, or violence, do not treat that merely as a “libido mismatch.” Seek appropriate safety and qualified help. Scripture must never be used to trap someone in abuse.
But for the couple sitting quietly in the ordinary ache of mismatched desire, hear this:
You are more than what is happening in your bedroom.
Your marriage is more than tonight.
And your story is not finished simply because this chapter hurts.
There is grace here.
Not cheap grace that pretends nothing is wrong.
Grace that gives courage to tell the truth.
Grace that makes confession possible.
Grace that softens defensiveness.
Grace that teaches wounded people how to listen again.
Grace that allows a husband to say, “I have been selfish.”
Grace that allows a wife to say, “I stopped telling you what was happening inside me.”
Grace that allows either spouse to say, “I have punished you with silence.”
Grace that says, “Forgive me.”
And grace that answers:
“Let's begin again.”
That is the scandal of Christianity.
We do not worship a Savior who waited until His bride became perfect before loving her.
Scripture says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Christ moved toward the undeserving.
That does not mean tolerating destructive behavior.
It means Christian love is shaped by something greater than reciprocation.
And this is where your marriage problem suddenly exposes something even deeper.
Maybe you came to this article asking:
“What if my spouse doesn't want sex?”
But perhaps Jesus is asking:
“What is this pain revealing inside you?”
Fear?
Pride?
Entitlement?
Shame?
Bitterness?
Insecurity?
Resentment?
A desperate need to be validated?
An inability to communicate?
A wound you buried years ago?
Sin you have been hiding?
Whatever has surfaced, don't waste it.
Bring it to Christ.
The Gospel is not God helping decent people become slightly better spouses.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners separated from God can be reconciled to Him through Jesus Christ.
Jesus died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by being a perfect husband.
Salvation is not earned by becoming a sexually available wife.
You are not redeemed by fixing your marriage.
You are redeemed through Christ.
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures… And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.”
—1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV
So repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Speak where silence has become poisonous.
Listen where pride has made you deaf.
Get help where the wound is beyond what the two of you currently know how to repair.
And love your spouse as a person made in God's image—not as the gatekeeper of something you believe you deserve.
Sex matters.
But souls matter more.
Intimacy matters.
But Christ matters infinitely more.
And when Christ becomes the center rather than merely the referee of your marriage disputes, something changes.
Maybe not overnight.
Maybe your bedroom will not magically transform tomorrow.
Christian hope is not pretending complicated problems disappear after one prayer.
But two people continually surrendering themselves to Jesus can begin becoming different people.
Hard hearts can soften.
Hidden wounds can be named.
Sin can be confessed.
Trust can be rebuilt.
Affection can return.
Tenderness can grow.
And sometimes intimacy that seemed buried can slowly breathe again.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't hide behind embarrassment now.
And if Christ is restoring something you thought was dead, tell somebody. Your testimony may become the hope another marriage desperately needs tonight.
Not because every sentence will apply to every marriage, but because pain has a way of making us forget what we knew when we were thinking clearly.
But please remember this:
You do not share an article to earn heaven.
You do not purchase grace.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
We support Gospel work because we have received grace—not because we are trying to buy it.
And perhaps somebody on your Facebook feed is lying beside their spouse tonight feeling completely unwanted.
Perhaps somebody is silently wondering whether their marriage can survive.
Perhaps somebody is one lonely decision away from adultery.
Perhaps somebody has been pressuring a spouse and desperately needs conviction.
Perhaps somebody has been withdrawing for years because they are carrying a wound they have never found the courage to explain.
You may never know whose screen this reaches after you press “Share.”
But God does.
So send truth farther than your own timeline.
Let another wounded marriage know there is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still repentance.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still grace.
There is still Jesus.
Because the question was never merely whether your spouse wants sex tonight.
The deeper question is what Christ will do with two imperfect people who finally stop hiding their wounds from Him and from each other.

And maybe the bedroom you thought proved your marriage was dying will someday become the place where you remember the night two wounded people stopped demanding to be understood—and finally began learning how to love again.
Some stories look most hopeless one sentence before Jesus begins rewriting them.
